claims.text: Applying an ultrathin inert surface coating to nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs solid-solution catalysts will enhance durability during ethanol oxidation.
The coating will modulate the electronic environment at the catalyst surface.
The coating will suppress the accumulation of species that deactivate the catalyst.
An ultrathin oxide layer can serve as the proposed inert surface coating.
Coating-induced changes in local electronic interactions will reduce the adsorption strength of poisoning intermediates.
Reduced adsorption strength of poisoning intermediates will diminish the formation of carbonaceous deposits.
The coating acts as protective cladding that alters adsorption energies through electronic modulation of metal sites.
Altered adsorption energies will minimize irreversible surface poisoning during ethanol oxidation.
Minimizing irreversible surface poisoning will improve catalyst durability while retaining acceptable activity.
Relative to uncoated catalysts, coated catalysts will deactivate more slowly and have a longer catalytic lifetime.
The coating may cause a modest reduction or negligible change in initial catalytic activity.
The proposed mechanism is expected to hold from 60°C to 120°C, at atmospheric pressure, and at standard ethanol feed concentrations.
The results may differ at very high temperatures, drastically different pH values, or non-standard reactant concentrations.
